titulo: The two conjugations: The most common irregular verbs

aula.objetivo: Recognise the 1st and 2nd conjugations, conjugate verbs in the present tense without mixing up the endings, and learn the most common irregular verbs.

blocos.titulo: ADVERBS: the words that never change
blocos.explicacao: ADVERBS: the words that never change. Before we close this lesson, I need to introduce a class of words that will give you huge relief: adverbs. I'll be direct: the adverb is the easiest class of words in the whole of Russian. I am not exaggerating, and you will see why in three minutes. What is an adverb? An adverb is a word that modifies the verb. It tells you how, when, where or how often the action happens. You use adverbs all the time in English: I read quickly (how?). We arrived today (when?). He lives here (where?). She always studies (how often?). Quickly, today, here, always: all adverbs. They attach to the verb and tell you how, when or where the action happens. The big news: the adverb is INVARIABLE. Now pay attention to this word: invariable. It means: it does not change. Ever. For any reason. Let me prove it with concrete examples. Proof 1: the adverb does not change with gender. Take the English adverb "today". Does it change if the speaker is a man or a woman? "I am happy today" is the same for both. There is no "todayess" for a woman. Russian is the same. The adverb сего́дня (today) is always сего́дня, whether the speaker is a man, a woman, a child or an adult. Proof 2: the adverb does not change with number. Take "here". Does it change if one person or several are here? "I am here. We are here." No. "Here" is "here" for one or for a thousand. Russian is the same: здесь is always здесь. Proof 3: the adverb does not change with tense. Take "yesterday". It does not become anything else when the verb changes. Russian is the same. The adverb вчера́ (yesterday) is always вчера́. What changes is the verb, not the adverb: in the past tense «читал» changes to «читала» for a woman, but вчера́ stays put. The golden rule of the adverb: an adverb is a frozen word. It does not change with gender, number, person, tense or case. It is always the same form, in any sentence, with any subject, in any context. That is why the adverb is the easiest class in Russian. While nouns, adjectives and verbs change form, adverbs stand still. If you like memorising, memorise adverbs. There are no tricks, no exceptions, no conjugation. It is the only class in Russian where you can learn a word and use it for ever without fear. Some essential adverbs. Here are the most used adverbs in everyday life; notice that all are invariable. Time. Place. Manner. How to use adverbs in sentences. The position of the adverb is flexible. Generally: an adverb of time goes before the verb or at the start of the sentence. An adverb of place goes after the verb. An adverb of manner goes after the verb. Examples follow. Notice that the adverb never changes form, whatever the sentence. Хорошо́ is always хорошо́. Сего́дня is always сего́дня. Здесь is always здесь. You do not need to think about gender, number, person or tense. Just drop the word in. Comparison with English: you already do this. In English the adverb is invariable too: I speak well. She speaks well. We speak well. They speak well. "Well" is always "well". The difference: in English many adverbs are made from adjectives by adding "-ly" (slow → slowly, quick → quickly). In Russian many adverbs are made from adjectives by changing the ending to -о (or -е): хоро́ший → хорошо́, бы́стрый → бы́стро. But that is only the origin of the adverb. Once formed, it stands still. Хорошо́ does not become anything else for a woman or for a plural. It is always хорошо́. Full stop. An important remark: adverb versus neuter adjective. Be careful not to confuse the adverb with the neuter adjective. They can have the same form but different jobs. Он хорошо́ говори́т. (He speaks well.) → хорошо́ is an adverb: it modifies the verb говори́т. Э́то хоро́шее вино́. (This is a good wine.) → хоро́шее is a neuter adjective: it modifies the noun вино́. The difference is in the job: if it modifies a verb, it is an adverb; if it modifies a noun, it is an adjective. Context makes this clear. Quick exercise. Complete with the right adverb. • 1. Я ____ чита́ю. (now) • 2. Он ____ рабо́тает. (today) • 3. Мы бу́дем ____ в Москве́. (tomorrow) • 4. Я был ____ в теа́тре. (yesterday) • 5. Она́ живёт ____. (there) • 6. Он ____ чита́ет. (here) • 7. Я ____. (at home) • 8. Она́ ____ говори́т по-ру́сски. (well) • 9. Он ____ чита́ет. (slowly) • 10. Они́ ____ рабо́тают. (always) Answer key: • 1. сейча́с • 2. сего́дня • 3. за́втра • 4. вчера́ • 5. там • 6. здесь (or тут) • 7. до́ма • 8. хорошо́ • 9. ме́дленно • 10. всегда́. Pocket summary: adverbs. • 1. An adverb is a word that modifies the verb (it says how, when, where, how often). • 2. The adverb is invariable. It does not change with gender, number, person, tense or case. • 3. "Today" is today for a man, a woman, a child, an adult. Always. • 4. "Here" is here for one person or a thousand. Always. • 5. "Well" is well for any subject. Always. • 6. If you like memorising, memorise adverbs. They are the easiest class in Russian: no conjugation, no declension, no tricks. Just use them. • 7. The most essential: сейча́с, сего́дня, за́втра, вчера́, всегда́, никогда́, здесь, там, до́ма, хорошо́, пло́хо, бы́стро, ме́дленно.

blocos.titulo: Consonant mutation and a summary of the two conjugations
blocos.explicacao: Consonant mutation in verbs, and a summary chart of the two conjugations in the present. Some verbs change the last consonant of the stem. In the second conjugation the change usually happens only in the я form (люблю́ but лю́бишь, лю́бят). In the first conjugation (for example писа́ть) the changed consonant stays in all forms (пишу́, пи́шешь, пи́шут). English has a faint echo of this ("office" and "officer", "electric" and "electricity", where k becomes s), but in Russian it is regular and predictable. blocos.titulo: The irregular verbs you will use most
blocos.explicacao: Few verbs break the rule, but they appear every day. Memorise these forms. Careful: the verb «есть» (to eat) is different from the «есть» of «У меня есть» (there is, exists): «Я ем суп» (I eat soup) × «У меня есть суп» (I have soup). «Идти» and «хотеть» appeared in earlier lessons.

blocos.titulo: Что ты пьёшь? / What are you drinking?
blocos.contexto: Two friends are chatting by voice message.

linhas.pt: — Hi, Max! What are you drinking?

linhas.ru: — Я пью кофе. Ты ешь утром?
linhas.pt: — I drink coffee. Do you eat in the morning?
linhas.audio: Я пью кофе. Ты ешь утром?

linhas.ru: — Нет, утром я не ем. Я пью чай.
linhas.pt: — No, I don't eat in the morning. I drink tea.
linhas.audio: Нет, утром я не ем. Я пью чай.

linhas.pt: — Can you work in the evening?
— Yes, I can. In the evening I'm at home.

blocos.enunciado: Say: «Я пью воду. Я не ем утром. Я могу работать. Я сплю поздно.»
